{"id": "16:68/q13", "question": "What does 'what they raise' refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the context of bee habitation restricts raised structures to hives and buildings, allows vineyards, or leaves the class broad.", "positions": [{"id": "16:68/q13/p1", "position": "Human-made bee shelters, especially hives, roofs, walls, and other buildings.", "reasons": "Al-Farra, al-Tabari as reported by al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Alusi, al-Wahidi, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Study Quran refer it to people's building and roofing. {"id": "16:68/q14", "question": "What happened when bees received this inspiration?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different events and practices.", "positions": [{"id": "16:68/q14/p1", "position": "A report says the bee was inspired in honey-making on Eid al-Fiṭr, the Day of Mercy.", "reasons": "Bursevi attributes the report to ʿAjāʾib al-Makhlūqāt."}, {"id": "16:68/q14/p2", "position": "People move bees to pasture, travel with them, and the bees follow.", "reasons": "Al-Durr cites this account alongside livestock made subject to humans at 36:71–72."}]}
{"id": "16:68/q15", "question": "What reports describe the bee's special standing?", "turns_on": "The reports concern distinct claims.", "positions": [{"id": "16:68/q15/p1", "position": "A report says all flies are in the Fire except bees.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi cites Abu Hurayra's Prophetic report recorded by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul; Bursevi repeats the saying as a mark of the honeybee's distinction."}, {"id": "16:68/q15/p2", "position": "A Prophetic report forbids killing bees along with ants, hoopoes, and shrikes.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi gives Ibn Abbas as transmitter, Abu Dawud as recorder, and says the issue recurs in the ant passage."}]}
{"id": "16:68/q16", "question": "What rulings are reported about eating and killing bees?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:68/q16/p1", "position": "Eating bees is forbidden though honey is lawful; killing bees is disliked.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites Hayat al-Hayawan and compares lawful human milk with forbidden human flesh; al-Qurtubi cites the Prophetic prohibition on killing bees."}]}
{"id": "16:68/q17", "question": "May bees be sold?", "turns_on": "Whether bees can be treated as saleable property, with visibility or exposure conditions.", "positions": [{"id": "16:68/q17/p1", "position": "Sale is valid when all bees in the hive are visible, and valid if sold exposed.", "reasons": "Bursevi attributes these rulings to al-Tatimma."}, {"id": "16:68/q17/p2", "position": "Sale of exposed bees is invalid.", "reasons": "Bursevi says al-Tahdhib gives the opposite ruling from al-Tatimma on exposed bees."}, {"id": "16:68/q17/p3", "position": "Sale of bees is invalid, like sale of wasps and other insects.", "reasons": "Bursevi attributes this to Abu Hanifa, who nevertheless allows sale of silkworms for silk."}]}
{"id": "16:68/q18", "question": "How does the bee passage connect to surrounding verses and the sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:68/q18/p1", "position": "It follows food and drink signs as a culminating proof of God's power, wisdom, and purposeful creation.", "reasons": "Al-Razi links milk and the drinks from dates and grapes in 16:66–67 with honey. {"id": "16:68/q20", "question": "Is the bee read as a symbol of ʿAlī and the Prophet's family?", "turns_on": "Whether Ali's title yaʿsub warrants taking the bee and its drink as symbols of his family and teachings.", "positions": [{"id": "16:68/q20/p1", "position": "Yes: the bee is ʿAlī and the family, and its diverse drink is their Quranic knowledge and wisdom that heals spiritually.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this from some Shiite commentators; al-Tabrisi traces it to Ali's saying he was the believers' yaʿsub, a word for both male bee and leader. {"id": "16:69/q18", "question": "How broad is honey's promised healing?", "turns_on": "Whether the indefinite healing and 'for people' imply some effective cases or universal efficacy.", "positions": [{"id": "16:69/q18/p1", "position": "Honey heals in some illnesses and people, or in many usual cases; no remedy must cure everyone.", "reasons": "Muqatil says some illnesses. {"id": "16:69/q19", "question": "What force does the indefinite 'healing' carry?", "turns_on": "Whether indefiniteness limits scope or conveys grandeur.", "positions": [{"id": "16:69/q19/p1", "position": "It marks some healing, leaving room for cases honey does not cure.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Burhan and Alusi give this possibility; Qurtubi says an affirmative indefinite has no universal force by agreement of language and law scholars; Ibn Kathir reports the same medical reading."}, {"id": "16:69/q19/p2", "position": "It magnifies the striking healing found in honey.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Burhan and Alusi also give this rhetorical possibility; Alusi says the surprising medicine comes from a stinging, possibly venomous creature."}]}
{"id": "16:69/q20", "question": "What happened when honey was prescribed for the man's ill brother?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:69/q20/p1", "position": "The Prophet repeatedly told the man to give honey for his brother's stomach illness or diarrhea; after further doses the brother recovered.", "reasons": "Yahya, Abd al-Razzaq, Tabari, Thalabi, Mawardi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Ibn Jawzi, Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Durr, Bursevi, Alusi and Study Quran cite the report. {"id": "16:69/q22", "question": "What other reports and practices illustrate honey's healing?", "turns_on": "The notes give distinct reports and practices rather than one single incident.", "positions": [{"id": "16:69/q22/p1", "position": "Honey and the Quran are called the two cures, for bodily illness and what is in hearts.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud's statement is cited widely, sometimes with an exhortation to use both. {"id": "16:69/q23", "question": "Does the healing verse allow medical treatment?", "turns_on": "Whether seeking a remedy belongs to trust in divine decree or conflicts with the ideal of reliance.", "positions": [{"id": "16:69/q23/p1", "position": "Treatment with medicines and permitted ruqya is lawful and can be part of God's decree.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says the verse supports treatment, as does Study Quran; most scholars allow treatment and ruqya, Malik explicitly. {"id": "16:69/q26", "question": "How does the bee community function?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:69/q26/p1", "position": "Bee groups follow a leader, coordinate their movements, and display remarkable ordered behavior.", "reasons": "Baghawi and Qurtubi say the ya'sub stops and moves with the group; Tabarsi says the leader protects, directs and governs, and loss of it disrupts order. {"id": "16:69/q27", "question": "What moral comparisons do reports draw between a bee and a believer?", "turns_on": "The comparisons emphasize either useful purity or the humble origin of prized goods.", "positions": [{"id": "16:69/q27/p1", "position": "A believer, like a bee, takes wholesome things and produces benefit without harm.", "reasons": "Durr gives Ibn Umar's and Prophetic comparisons, including Bilal taking bitter and sweet yet producing sweetness; al-Tabarani's chain is good and al-Hakim authenticates a related report. {"id": "16:69/q30", "question": "How does the bee sign relate to neighboring signs and the surah?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the verse to the drinks sequence, surah naming, and differing levels of perception.", "positions": [{"id": "16:69/q30/p1", "position": "The bee completes a sequence of divinely given drinks and blessings before ethical instruction.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan compares honey with milk and fruit drinks. {"id": "16:69/q33", "question": "What inward lessons are drawn from the bee's food and honey?", "turns_on": "The inward notes apply different parts of the bee's work to distinct stages, conduct, and divine inspiration.", "positions": [{"id": "16:69/q33/p1", "position": "Honey heals souls, while the heart and spirit require deeper disciplines and witnessing.", "reasons": "Sulami distinguishes soul healing from heart nourishment through attention, humility and retreat, and spirit nourishment through witnessing and hearing God without created distractions."}, {"id": "16:69/q33/p2", "position": "The obedient believer becomes a source of healing to others like the bee.", "reasons": "Abu Bakr al-Warraq says guarding the inward secret and turning to God make sight, speech and company healing. {"id": "16:96/q03", "question": "What do 'what you have' and 'what is with God' denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the contrast concerns material goods, deeds and recompense, or human and divine spiritual qualities.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q03/p1", "position": "People's worldly possessions or enjoyment perish; God's lasting reward, afterlife, or Paradise endures.", "reasons": "Muqātil mentions wealth and afterlife reward; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes an owner may die before goods expire. {"id": "16:96/q08", "question": "Does a persistent thing need a distinct attribute of persistence?", "turns_on": "Whether persistence is bare continued existence or an added quality.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q08/p1", "position": "No; persistence is continued existence itself.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī and Abū Hāshim say no added quality is required; al-Ṭabrisī attributes the same answer to most theologians."}, {"id": "16:96/q08/p2", "position": "Yes; a thing persists through a distinct attribute of baqāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī attributes this to Abū al-Qāsim; al-Ṭabrisī attributes it to al-Balkhī."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q09", "question": "Does substance persist?", "turns_on": "Whether persistence applies to all substances or only some.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q09/p1", "position": "Substance persists, and in one formulation all substance does.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports the first from most exegetes and the universal claim from the Ḥashwiyya."}, {"id": "16:96/q09/p2", "position": "Some substance persists and some does not.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports his teachers' position, adding that they differ over details."}, {"id": "16:96/q09/p3", "position": "Not all substance persists.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports Abū Hāshim's denial of universality."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q10", "question": "Why use the nominal form bāqin?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q10/p1", "position": "The noun form signals permanence more strongly than a present-tense verb.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī draws the implication from the wording."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q11", "question": "How is the reward verb read?", "turns_on": "Whether the promise turns to direct divine speech or continues reference to God in the third person.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q11/p1", "position": "With first-person plural nūn: 'We shall reward,' a majestic divine self-reference and shift to direct speech.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and ʿĀṣim recur across the sources; some include Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Dhakwān, or Yaʿqūb, and reports from Abū ʿAmr differ. Al-Fārisī says it has the same meaning as yāʾ and notes unanimous nūn in 16:97."}, {"id": "16:96/q11/p2", "position": "With third-person yāʾ: 'He shall reward,' referring back to God.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī and al-Ṭabrisī connect the pronoun to 'what is with God remains'; Ibn ʿĀshūr links it to God as the one forbidding, promising, and rewarding. The majority or remaining readers have this form, with reported differences over named readers."}]}
{"id": "16:96/q12", "question": "What makes the reward promise emphatic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q12/p1", "position": "The oath lām and emphatic nūn make it a solemn divine promise.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls it God's oath. {"id": "16:96/q13", "question": "Who are 'those who were patient,' and what did they endure?", "turns_on": "Whether the patience names covenant fidelity and obedience, endurance of persecution, or the discipline underlying every duty.", "positions": [{"id": "16:96/q13/p1", "position": "They remain faithful to God and His covenant, obey commands, and avoid prohibitions despite hardship or temptation.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Baghawī and al-Ṭabrisī emphasize covenant keeping; Ibn ʿAṭiyya specifies desire for prohibited earnings.
